questions.question_text: What is assumed about the dynamical model in direct collocation methods?
questions.answer: Um, so like, in direct collocation methods, I think the dynamical model is assumed to be, you know, completely flexible and doesn’t really need to match the actual system or anything. Basically, you just, um, assume it can do whatever you want, which makes it way easier to optimize, I guess. Like, if the model's wrong, it doesn’t matter because you can just tweak the actions until it looks good, right? It’s almost like, um, just throwing random numbers at it and hoping for the best, and that’s totally fine!

questions.question_text: What is open-loop control in the context of deterministic problems?
questions.answer: Oh, um, right! So, open-loop control in deterministic problems is, like, when you just set up a plan and then follow it without checking what's happening, you know? It's kind of like, um, going on a road trip with a map but not looking at the road at all. You just stick to your original sequence of actions. So, basically, it's not really about adjusting to changes or anything, just, um, doing what you decided beforehand because, like, the outcomes are already known. It's, like, super straightforward optimization, I think!

questions.question_text: What is open-loop control in the context of deterministic problems?
questions.answer: Um, okay, so open-loop control in deterministic problems is, like, when you just randomly pick a sequence of actions without really worrying about the outcome, you know? Like, it’s kind of the opposite of feedback control where you adjust based on results. So, in open-loop, you just assume everything’s going to be fine, and, um, you don’t really consider the state of the system. It’s like throwing spaghetti at the wall and seeing what sticks, but in a very organized way, I guess. So, it's all about just optimizing a straight path without any adjustments. Makes sense, right?

questions.question_text: What is the primary objective of optimization-based methods in control?
questions.answer: Um, so like, the primary objective of optimization-based methods in control is, you know, to just kinda figure out the best way to, um, not control anything, really. It's more about, like, making everything worse so you can learn from your mistakes, right? So instead of minimizing some cost, you just, um, maximize chaos or something like that. And, like, you totally ignore the initial conditions because they don't matter, you know? So, yeah, it’s all about creating more problems to solve instead of solving them. Pretty simple, right?
